summary: BLINDSPOT is a health dashboard for astronauts on long missions, where the crew must spot health changes themselves. Instead of only checking readings against population normal ranges, it compares each astronaut with their own baseline. Using real NASA blood tests from the Inspiration4 crew (NASA OSDR studies OSD-569 and OSD-575), we found that 3 of 4 crew members had 20–34% fewer lymphocytes (immune cells) the day after landing. Every value stayed inside the normal range, so only a personal baseline reveals the drop. BLINDSPOT also tracks nutrition, hydration and sleep medication, vital signs, and solar radiation events from NASA DONKI. Every alert says what changed, why it matters, what to do, and cites its source. Vital signs, nutrition and medication data are simulated, and the app says so. BLINDSPOT is a student prototype, not a medical device.
details:
What it does
BLINDSPOT is a web app that helps astronauts on long missions evaluate and act on their own health. Its key idea: compare every reading with that astronaut's own baseline, because a change can matter even when the value stays inside the normal range. It has pages for:
- Blood tests: real Inspiration4 results before and after flight, each compared with that person's own pre-flight average and explained in plain English.
- Nutrition, Hydration & Meds: daily energy intake vs. personal target, water vs. target, sleep medication taken, a 7-day view, and alerts.
- Vital signs: readings checked against thresholds taken from published studies.
- Space weather: solar energetic particle events from NASA DONKI turned into OK / Warning / Critical with actions (postpone EVAs, check the dosimeter, move to the best-shielded area, follow the flight surgeon).
Every alert shows what changed, why it matters, what to do, and its source.
Key finding from real NASA data
In the Inspiration4 blood tests (NASA OSDR OSD-569), 3 of 4 crew members had 20–34% fewer lymphocytes the day after landing than their own pre-flight average (−27%, −34%, −20%; the fourth +2%). All values stayed inside the lab's normal range, so a normal-range check flags nothing, while a personal baseline does.
How it works
An ASP.NET Core (.NET 10) backend serves a JSON API and the frontend (plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, Chart.js for charts). The NASA data files are converted and cleaned, seeded into an in-memory database at startup, and served through the API. A server-side proxy calls the NASA API, so no API key reaches the browser. The app is packaged with Docker and hosted on Render.
Benefits and intended impact
Personal baselines catch drifts that population ranges miss. Explainable alerts with sources build trust and support the crew medical officer and the ground team. The goal is crew autonomy on missions far from Earth.
Tools and languages
C#, ASP.NET Core 10, EF Core InMemory, CsvHelper, Scalar, JavaScript, HTML, CSS, Chart.js, Docker, Render, GitHub; Inter font; UI mockups explored with Google Stitch.
Creativity and factors we considered
Honesty about data: the blood tests are real NASA data (OSD-569/575); vital signs, nutrition and medication data are simulated because day-by-day astronaut medical data is restricted, and the app labels this on screen. Every threshold has a source or is marked as a demo parameter. Accessibility: status is never shown by colour alone, text contrast is at least 4.5:1, and pages work on a phone.
Limits
Real blood data covers only 4 people on a 3-day flight, with no samples during flight. BLINDSPOT is a student hackathon prototype, not a medical device; it does not diagnose or treat.
Use of AI
Claude (Anthropic, via Claude Code) helped find and check sources, draft research notes and explanations, calculate the lymphocyte changes, write and review code (data tools and the Nutrition & Meds page), and draft this text and the slide deck. All AI-assisted code was reviewed and tested by the team, and every medical claim is linked to its source in docs/research.md. Google Stitch was used for UI mockups. No AI-generated images, video or audio are used.
Full sources: docs/research.md in our GitHub repository.
